name: Nystatin
route_note: oral suspension or pastilles held in the mouth (not systemically absorbed); creams, ointments and powders; vaginal tablets
originator: New York State Department of Health (Elizabeth Lee Hazen and Rachel Fuller Brown); licensed to E. R. Squibb & Sons

discovery.by: Elizabeth Lee Hazen and Rachel Fuller Brown
discovery.note: Isolated from Streptomyces noursei found in soil from a farm in Virginia; named after the New York State Department of Health.

tagline: First useful polyene antifungal, still used for oral thrush and skin candidiasis
summary: Nystatin is a polyene antifungal produced by Streptomyces noursei and was the first antifungal of its class to be used clinically. It is too toxic for injection and is not absorbed from the gut, so it is used only on the skin and mucous membranes. Its main uses are oral thrush, candidiasis of the skin and vaginal candidiasis.
mechanism: Like amphotericin B, nystatin binds ergosterol in fungal membranes and forms channels that let potassium and other small molecules leak out, killing the cell.
Because almost none is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract or intact skin, it acts locally and causes few systemic effects. Resistance in Candida is uncommon.
uses: Prevention of oral candidiasis in some immunocompromised or neonatal patients

history.title: Collaboration
history.detail: Hazen, in New York City, and Brown, in Albany, begin screening soil actinomycetes for antifungal activity.

history.title: Discovery
history.detail: Hazen and Brown, working by mail between New York City and Albany, report the antifungal 'fungicidin', renamed nystatin.

history.title: Amphotericin B
history.detail: A second polyene, amphotericin B, is discovered; it becomes the systemic polyene of choice while nystatin remains topical and oral.

history.title: Inventors' Hall of Fame
history.detail: Hazen and Brown are inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame.

pk.bioavailability: negligible from gut, skin and mucosa

common: nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea at high oral doses

facts: The name nystatin comes from 'New York State', where its discoverers worked.
Hazen and Brown gave their royalties to the non-profit Research Corporation to fund scientific research.
Nystatin was also used to treat fungal damage to art and historic buildings, including after the 1966 Florence flood.
